faqs.question: Who should actually get a Diwali wish with their name and photo on it?
faqs.answer: The eight to ten people whose reaction you would genuinely notice: parents and grandparents, the siblings and cousins you actually talk to, a partner, and the few close friends who live elsewhere. Everyone else on a fifty-name Diwali list is better served by one warm line sent individually, with no graphic at all.

faqs.question: When should I send Diwali wishes with a name and photo in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: Diwali (Lakshmi Puja) falls on Sunday 8 November 2026, in a festival running from Dhanteras on Friday 6 November to Bhai Dooj on Wednesday 11 November. Send the personal ones on Saturday 7 November or early Sunday, before the broadcast wave. Diwali 2027 is Friday 29 October, a working day, so send on the evening.

faqs.question: Is a name-on-image JPG or a shareable page better for a Diwali greeting?
faqs.answer: A JPG is the right tool for the broadcast tier because it costs seconds and needs no explanation. A page is worth the twenty minutes only for the few people you want to say something specific to, and it has to work on a phone: 51.8% of the 33,007 views on SubhSandesh pages are mobile (measured 2026-08-19).

faqs.question: Does putting someone's name on a Diwali greeting actually make them appreciate it more?
faqs.answer: Less than senders expect. In Zhang and Epley's 2012 experiments, the effort a giver put in had no measurable effect on how receivers rated the gift (7.22 versus 7.39), while givers confidently predicted it would. The effort paid the giver in felt closeness, not the recipient.

faqs.question: What photo should I use on a Diwali greeting with their name?
faqs.answer: Two or three photos of your own family or of the two of you, not a stock diya or rangoli. Aknin and Human's six studies found both givers and receivers feel greater closeness from gifts that reflect the giver. Pages that hold up to six photos do not need all six filled; real ones beat many.

faqs.question: How do I send a personalised Diwali page privately instead of to a group?

faqs.question: Is it rude to send the same Diwali message to colleagues and clients?
faqs.answer: No, and it is better than the alternative. A colleague does not need their name burned into a diya graphic; what registers is that the message was sent individually rather than forwarded to a list, so write one specific line and send it one at a time.

faqs.question: How many Diwali greetings do people usually send?
faqs.answer: There is no Diwali figure, but Hill and Dunbar's card study is the closest measure: 43 households sent a mean of 68 cards each, ranging from 11 to 149, reaching 153.5 people on average. A Diwali contact list behaves like the upper end of that.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Diwali Wishes With Name and Photo: Who Should Get One

Diwali wishes with name and photo are worth making for the eight or ten people whose reaction you would actually notice; send everyone else something plain and warm. Diwali is a broadcast festival: the average Christmas-card sender in [Hill and Dunbar's study of 2,984 cards](https://rahill.webspace.durham.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/207/2021/04/Hill-and-Dunbar-2003.pdf) posted 68 cards, and a Diwali list is rarely shorter. Personalised pages behave nothing like that. Across 2,739 pages created on SubhSandesh since 2026-03-12, the average page collects 12.1 views, and 44.3% of creators password-protect the page before sharing it — both measured 2026-08-19. Those are numbers from an artefact made for a handful of people, not a mailing list.

## What a Diwali wish with a name and photo actually is

It is a greeting carrying the recipient's name and at least one photograph, so it could not have been sent unchanged to anyone else. It comes in two formats: a flat image with the name rendered into the artwork, and a web page with names, photos and a message, shared as a link.

The format decides what the recipient can do with it. An image sits in their gallery. A page can hold several photos, a longer message and a password, which 1,213 of 2,739 SubhSandesh creators chose to add before sharing (measured 2026-08-19).

## Diwali is a broadcast festival, so the maths is different

Raksha Bandhan is one-to-one. Diwali is one-to-fifty: parents, siblings, cousins, the school group, colleagues, clients, the neighbour. Hill and Dunbar's 43 respondents sent a mean of 68 cards each, with a range from 11 to 149, and the individuals contacted numbered 153.5 on average.

The more useful finding is what governed contact: once distance and work ties were controlled for, **emotional closeness** predicted how often two people were in touch. Your list is not flat, and the greeting should not be either.

Lakshmi Puja falls on **Sunday 8 November 2026**, inside a festival running from Dhanteras on Friday 6 November to Bhai Dooj on Wednesday 11 November, so the whole broadcast tier fires at roughly the same hour on a day nobody is at work. Send the personal ones a day early. Diwali 2027 falls on **Friday 29 October**, a working day, which moves the crush to the evening.

## Who on your list actually warrants a name and a photo

Five tiers, in the order we would spend effort on them. Each says roughly how long it takes.

### 1. Parents and grandparents

The people who will open it twice and show it to someone else. Use the name they are actually called — Amma, Papa, Nani — and a photo they appear in, ideally one they have not seen. Twenty to thirty minutes, written from scratch.

### 2. Your siblings and the cousins you genuinely talk to

Usually three to six people out of a cousin group of thirty. A photo from a shared Diwali does the work a written message cannot, and siblings read formal wording as distance. Ten to fifteen minutes each.

### 3. A partner

The highest-return single greeting on the list. Personalise the photos and the letter, skip the clip-art, and say one thing about this year nobody else could. About twenty minutes.

### 4. Close friends who live somewhere else

Four or five people, typically the ones distance has quietly downgraded. Their name and one photo of the two of you is enough; ten minutes each. A link suits this tier because it survives being reopened in December, after the gallery has been cleared.

### 5. Colleagues, clients, neighbours and the wider list

Thirty to forty people, none of whom need their name on a diya graphic. Write one warm, specific line with their name in it, send it individually, and skip photos — your family in a client's WhatsApp is a small imposition. Under a minute each.

## What a name buys you when the recipient knows you sent forty-nine others

Less than most senders assume. In [Zhang and Epley's experiments in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General](https://web2-bschool.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/media_rp/publications/we48l1424841808.pdf) (2012), the effort a giver put into choosing a gift had no measurable effect on how receivers rated it — 7.22 versus 7.39 on their scale, statistically indistinguishable — while givers confidently expected the thoughtful choice to land better.

Zhang and Epley's argument is that thought only counts when something *triggers* the recipient to consider it. A greeting arriving in a stack of thirty on the same Sunday afternoon is the opposite of a trigger.

This is also where personalisation starts to look automated. [Gino and Flynn's five studies](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/publications/give-them-what-they-want-benefits-explicitness-gift-exchange) (Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, September 2011) found recipients appreciated gifts they had explicitly asked for more than unsolicited ones, while givers assumed both would land equally.

A name auto-inserted into forty graphics is unprompted effort of the cheapest kind. One page for one person reads differently because it visibly could not have been mass-produced.

## Which photo to use, and why a family photo behaves differently

The name-on-image generators we read on this results page in August 2026 hand you a diya, rangoli or fireworks backdrop and drop the recipient's face into a frame. [SFU's summary of Aknin and Human's six studies](https://www.sfu.ca/fass/news/2017/02/study--giving-a-gift-that-reflects-you-rather-than-your-valentin/) (Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2015) reports that although people prefer gifts reflecting the *recipient*, both sides felt greater closeness from gifts that reflected the *giver*. A photo of your own family lighting diyas discloses something; a stock diya, or the recipient's cropped face on festival artwork, discloses nothing.

There is a second trap. [Steffel, Williams and LeBoeuf's working paper](https://marketing.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/Steffel-Williams-LeBoeuf-April-2015.pdf) (April 2015) found 65% of givers picked a store-specific gift card over a general one against 26% of recipients, and only 18% of givers thought the general card was the more thoughtful choice versus 45% of recipients.

Over-specifying is a giver's instinct. Two or three real photos beat six and a nickname, even when the format has room for six.

## How SubhSandesh's Diwali page holds two names and up to six photos

As of October 2026, SubhSandesh has a Diwali page built around exactly this search. You add their name and yours and choose love, family or a friend; the default wishes, blessing and reply follow that choice, and every line stays editable.

What the recipient does is the point. They light a diya at their door that carries a tag from you, then a row of diyas that each lift one of your wishes. They colour a rangoli until your initials glow, write the word you chose in the air with a sparkler, and light paper sky lanterns holding up to six of your photos.

Crackers are drawn by the page, so there is no noise or smoke. Your letter opens from a red-and-gold shagun liffafa, and a box of mithai opens onto a Shubh Deepavali card signed by you, which they can save as a 1080×1920 image.

Add a YouTube song or a Diwali favourite, or let the AI write the wishes from a few lines about you both. The template's guide puts the build at about five minutes; it goes out as a private link that opens in any browser, with no app or account.

For anyone in tiers one to four, start with the [SubhSandesh Diwali page with names and photos](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali). If what you want to tell a partner is not really about Diwali, the [romantic "I love you" page](https://subhsandesh.in/love-gf) fits better: it is the most-made page on the site, 914 of 2,739 created (measured 2026-08-19).

## Five recipient tiers matched to a format

SubhSandesh's own measurements sit in the last column, all taken 2026-08-19.

| Recipient tier | What to send | Where the name goes | Photos | SubhSandesh measurement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parents and grandparents | Diwali page, family setting | Diya tag, as Amma or Papa | 1–3 they appear in | 51.8% of page views are on a phone (17,101 of 33,007) |
| Siblings and close cousins | Diwali page, family setting | Both names, initials in the rangoli | Up to 6 from shared Diwalis | 12.1 average views per created page |
| A partner | Diwali page, love setting | The letter in the liffafa | 2–3 of the two of you | Median 6.9 hours between first save and last edit |
| Close friends far away | Diwali page, friend setting | Diya tag | 1 of the two of you | 44.3% of creators add a password (1,213 of 2,739) |
| Colleagues, clients, wider list | One written line, sent individually | First word of the message | None | None: sent outside the platform |

Effort scales with closeness, and with over half of views on a phone, whatever you build must work on a 6-inch screen first.

## When a name and photo is the wrong choice

If the recipient has no smartphone, a link is worse than a printed card and a phone call — 51.8% of views being mobile is a fact about the medium, not an argument for it. If you are in the same house on 8 November, a greeting page is a strange substitute for saying शुभ दीपावली (*Shubh Deepavali*, "auspicious Diwali") over the diyas.

If a photo would embarrass the recipient in a work group, the plain line wins. The Diwali page has limits too: it is built for one person at a time, so it is wrong for the tier-five list, and someone wanting a still card to glance at once will find its interactive scenes more than they asked for.

The median creator keeps editing for 6.9 hours between first save and last edit (sampled on /love-gf, n=914, measured 2026-08-19). Build yours by Dhanteras — Friday 6 November in 2026, Wednesday 27 October in 2027 — so Diwali itself is a send and not a build.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page on this query that tells a reader to personalise fewer greetings, backs that with measured card-sending volumes and giver-versus-recipient experiments the generators never touch, and now ends on a real Diwali name-and-photo product (SubhSandesh's /happy-diwali, described only from its own JSON-LD) mapped tier by tier. The weakness remains that the first-party numbers are platform-wide August 2026 figures, not Diwali data (none exists for a page launched in October 2026), and domain authority is far below the name-on-image generators that own this SERP — a months-long play, not a ranking prediction.
